factors_up: OpenAI Deployment Co. (11 May) signals confident enterprise push — increases incentive to declare capability milestone (+1pp)

forecasts.question: Will economic consultancy lose ≥33% value/jobs by end 2030 due to AI?
forecasts.key_change: Hold at 25%. No fresh sector-level news in past 24 hours. Latest tracking still anchored to McKinsey's ~10% non-client headcount plan (a few thousand layoffs over 18-24 months), an additional 200-role cut in late 2025, and revenue stuck at $15-16B for five years. KPMG, Deloitte, Bain and Accenture continue similar AI-driven redesigns. McKinsey's own report finds 30% of companies planning AI-related layoffs in 2026. Still well short of 33% sector decline by 2030, but trajectory is consistent with the medium-tail of the distribution.
forecasts.base_rate: ~20-25% — historical sector contractions of >33% over 6 years are rare (~10-15% base rate); AI-specific disruption pushes this up given the cognitive-labour exposure of consultancy
factors_up: McKinsey ~10% non-client layoffs being executed; signals AI substitution at scale (+2pp)
Industry-wide pattern (KPMG/Deloitte/Bain/Accenture) of AI-driven workforce redesign (+2pp)
Revenue stagnation at McKinsey ($15-16B flat for 5 years) suggests genuine demand erosion, not just supply-side AI (+1pp)
30% of companies planning AI layoffs (McKinsey survey) — buy-side validation of consultancy disruption thesis (+1pp)
factors_down: Most cuts are non-client back-office roles; client-facing partner economics so far intact (-3pp)
33% decline is a high bar — requires structural collapse, not just AI-driven productivity (-3pp)
Sector capable of repricing toward AI-augmented delivery (per-seat economics) — revenue may hold even with fewer staff (-2pp)
Resolution requires 2+ credible analyses primarily attributing decline to AI — attribution challenge (-1pp)
key_uncertainties: Whether AI-driven productivity gains accrue to consultancies (margin uplift) or clients (price compression)
Whether McKinsey's job-cut trajectory accelerates into client-facing roles by 2027-2028
How analysts will attribute any decline (AI vs. macro vs. corporate de-consulting)

update_triggers.up: Big 4 / MBB announces >20% headcount reduction or revenue decline ≥10% in any single quarter, attributed to AI
update_triggers.down: Sector revenue rebounds; AI-augmented offerings drive premium pricing; client-facing roles stable through 2027

forecasts.question: Will Labour be largest party at next UK General Election?
forecasts.key_change: Hold at 3%. Crisis remains acute but unresolved: ~90 Labour MPs publicly calling for Starmer to resign or set a departure date, four junior ministers (Fahnbulleh, Jess Philips, Davies-Jones, Zubir Ahmed) resigned 12 May, four ministerial aides also out. A pro-Starmer letter signed by 103 MPs published 12 May provides a thin majority of named supporters. Starmer remains defiant at the 12 May cabinet meeting. A formal leadership contest requires 81 endorsements (20% of PLP); no formal challenge yet. CNBC Eurasia note says he is 'unlikely to last the year'. Whether Labour holds together until 2029 GE under any leader remains an open question; polling collapse from 2025/2026 locals and Mandelson scandal still binding. Underlying judgment: very low probability Labour can recover to be largest party by Dec 2029.
forecasts.base_rate: ~5-8% — mid-term collapsed-government parties have historically lost the following GE; the 2025-26 local collapse plus governance scandal makes recovery harder than typical mid-term troughs
factors_up: Time to election (Dec 2029) leaves ~3.5 years for recovery — long horizon for political mean reversion (+2pp)
Pro-Starmer letter with 103 MP signatures published 12 May suggests a stabilising floor of caucus support (+1pp)
Conservative and Reform UK fragmentation could allow Labour to win on a low vote share (+1pp)
factors_down: ~90 MPs publicly calling for resignation — mid-term confidence collapse rare to recover from before next GE (-3pp)
Four junior ministers resigning in one day signals accelerating crisis, not contained dissent (-2pp)
Mandelson appointment scandal compounds 2025/2026 local-election rout — two structural credibility hits (-2pp)
Eurasia Group / CNBC consensus that Starmer 'unlikely to last the year' implies fresh leadership contest, internal divisions, likely poll punishment (-2pp)
key_uncertainties: Whether the formal 81-MP threshold for a leadership contest is triggered in next 30 days
Whether a new leader (Cooper, Streeting, Burnham, Reeves) can credibly reset by 2027
Reform UK / Conservative dynamics on the right — whether the right consolidates or splits

update_triggers.up: Successful leadership transition with poll bounce >5pts; Conservative-Reform merger or pact collapses
update_triggers.down: Formal leadership challenge triggered; further mass resignations; polling falls below 20%

forecasts.question: Will UK annual CPI inflation fall below 2.0% for at least one month before 1 January 2027?
forecasts.key_change: Hold at 1%. ONS April 2026 CPI release is scheduled for 20 May 07:00 — not yet published. Last data point remains March 2026 at 3.3% (up from 3.0% in Feb 2026), with transport +4.7%, services +4.5%. Bank of England April MPR explicitly forecasts CPI between 3.0% and 3.5% in Q2-Q3 2026 due to higher energy prices flowing through from the Iran war shock. With only ~8 monthly prints (April-November 2026) remaining and the BoE's central path well above 2%, the conditional probability of any month printing below 2.0% is very low.
forecasts.base_rate: ~3-5% — when BoE forecasts a year of inflation in the 3-3.5% range, the modal outcome is no single sub-2% month. Sudden disinflationary shock would be needed.
factors_up: Energy prices could mean-revert sharply if Iran ceasefire holds and oil reverts to $60-70 (+1pp)
Services inflation could collapse if labour market loosens faster than BoE expects (+1pp)
Base effects in late 2026 from 2025's energy spike start to roll off (+1pp)
factors_down: BoE April MPR central path 3.0-3.5% Q2-Q3 2026 — no sub-2% month modelled (-3pp)
March 2026 print at 3.3% with services and transport elevated — broad-based pressure (-2pp)
Only ~8 monthly prints remain — limited dispersion windows for tail outcome (-2pp)
Iran-war energy shock has had only partial pass-through; further pressure likely (-1pp)
key_uncertainties: Whether Iran-war energy shock fully fades by autumn 2026
Whether services inflation breaks lower with labour-market softening
Whether the 20 May April-2026 print confirms BoE projection or surprises

update_triggers.up: April or May 2026 CPI prints below 2.5%; oil collapses to $50; BoE November 2026 MPR revises path sharply lower
update_triggers.down: April 2026 print at 3.5%+; further upside energy shock; wage growth re-accelerates

forecasts.question: Will UK average annual real GDP growth exceed 1.5% across the 2030s (2030-2039)?
forecasts.key_change: Hold at 39%. OBR March 2026 EFO remains the binding reference: GDP per person ~1.1% to 2030, productivity assumed to pick up to 1% medium term, labour-supply growth declining to ½% by 2030 driven by lower net migration and population ageing. Adding 1% productivity + ½% labour supply ≈ 1.5% headline GDP — i.e., right on the resolution threshold for the 2030s decade average. Public-sector net debt projected to stabilise at ~95% of GDP in early 2030s, leaving little fiscal headroom for growth stimulus. Trump-Xi summit and the Iran war energy shock add downside risk to global trade. Hold at 39%, reflecting balanced uncertainty around the threshold.
forecasts.base_rate: ~30-40% — historical UK decade-average real GDP growth has been above 1.5% only when productivity exceeded 1% (1990s, 2000s pre-GFC). Post-GFC trend has been around 1.3-1.5%; OBR central path now ~1.5%, putting probability mass either side of the threshold.
factors_up: OBR central path puts productivity at 1% medium term — sufficient with ½% labour supply to hit 1.5% (+3pp)
AI-driven productivity uplift remains an upside tail (genuine 1.5-2.0% productivity possible) (+2pp)
Public investment uplift (UK industrial strategy, capex) could lift TFP path (+1pp)
Sectoral rebalancing (energy, defence, services-exports) could improve trend (+1pp)
factors_down: Labour-supply growth declining to ½% by 2030 from population ageing and lower migration — secular drag (-3pp)
Productivity has structurally underperformed OBR for >15 years — base rate of OBR overestimating productivity is high (-2pp)
Iran-war energy shock raising terms-of-trade losses; persistent inflation drag (-1pp)
Public debt at 95% of GDP early 2030s limits fiscal scope to stimulate growth (-1pp)
Current UK political instability (Starmer crisis) increases policy-uncertainty premium (-1pp)
key_uncertainties: Whether AI productivity dividend lands in the UK or accrues primarily to US capex
Whether net migration policy stabilises to support labour supply
Whether productivity converges on 1%+ or stays at the 0.5% post-GFC trend

update_triggers.up: ONS productivity revisions upward; AI-driven sector data showing measurable productivity uplift; OBR November 2026 EFO raises trend
update_triggers.down: OBR cuts productivity assumption; further migration declines; persistent below-trend prints through 2027-28
